THE ABOUT US CONTRADICTION, addressed head-on: para 1 says the Gazette 'can be accessed free of cost by the general public being available in the public domain'; para 2 says the Controller is the authorised publisher/seller of the Gazette 'with its copy right' and 'Any infringement of the Indian Copyright Act is a legal offence'. These are reconcilable and should be read as: the Government asserts it OWNS copyright in the Gazette (para 2), while 'public domain' in para 1 is colloquial for 'freely publicly accessible', and the copyright/infringement assertion is aimed at protecting the Controller's separate commercial business of selling priced print publications ('quality product... economically priced... Dispute in Book trade'). The prudent posture for counsel is to ASSUME copyright subsists and rest reproduction on the statutory exception, not on the website wording. PRIMARY GROUND — s.52(1)(q)(i): reproduction or publication of 'any matter which has been published in any Official Gazette except an Act of a Legislature' is a permitted act, i.e. simply not an infringement. This is a statutory permission that operates regardless of the Controller's copyright claim — a s.52 permitted act cannot be defeated by an assertion of ownership. It squarely covers the gazette-notified instruments these three sources collect (notifications, rules, orders, directions, amendments). IMPORTANT: subordinate legislation notified in the Gazette (e.g. telecom rules/notifications, DoT/TRAI notifications) is 'matter published in the Official Gazette', NOT 'an Act of a Legislature' (which means primary legislation enacted by a legislature), so it falls inside (q)(i). THE (q)(ii) TRAP, flagged honestly: a BARE Act of a Legislature is excepted from (q)(i) and is permitted under s.52(1)(q)(ii) only if 'reproduced or published together with any commentary thereon or any other original matter'. A clean PDF of a bare Act with no commentary falls in the gap. For a Ministry gazette feed this is rare (the feed is overwhelmingly subordinate legislation), but if the archive ever captures a bare Act PDF, (q) does not cover it and the firm must fall back on fair dealing. METADATA DASHBOARD: needs NO exception at all. Under Eastern Book Company v. D.B. Modak (2008) 1 SCC 1, facts and short titles attract no copyright and their capture reproduces no substantial part under s.14; India has no sui generis database right. This limb is clean on facts-are-not-copyrightable grounds independently of s.52. PRIVATE PDF ARCHIVE: covered by s.52(1)(q)(i) for all gazette matter, with an independent backstop in s.52(1)(a) fair dealing for 'private or personal use, including research'. Per ANI Media v. CAVEAT: ANI is an interim order refusing an injunction, expressly prima facie, with no bearing on final outcome (para 274) and appealable — strong persuasive support, not settled law. GAZETTE-SPECIFIC REINFORCEMENT: IT Act s.8 makes the Electronic Gazette the authoritative statutory publication, so the archived record is the official instrument, not a secondary copy; and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 s.81 (carrying forward Evidence Act ss.81/81A) affords a presumption of genuineness to the electronic Gazette record, which gives the private archive genuine evidential value and makes archiving a legitimate professional purpose supporting the fairness limb. GODL-India is considered and does NOT apply (the Gazette is not published under NDSAP/GODL on data.gov.in). s.63 (knowing infringement, cognizable and non-bailable per Knit Pro, SC 2022) sets the ceiling: an internal, unpublished archive backed by (q)(i) plus documented fair dealing does not plausibly meet 'knowingly infringes'.

per_source.access_analysis: Analysed under the IT Act 2000. (1) EXPRESS PERMISSION: robots.txt = 'Allow: /' for all agents — the operator's authoritative, machine-readable crawl policy grants unconditional permission for every path (RFC 9309). No scraping clause exists in any policy; deep linking is expressly blessed. As a public authority MeitY also carries an RTI Act 2005 s.4(1)(b)/(2) proactive-disclosure duty over exactly this class of material, reinforcing implied permission. (2) WAF — MATERIAL CORRECTION TO THE 25-AUG PREMISE: the site is behind Akamai edge filtering. The registry states 'only an exact consumer-browser string is served; reaching it requires presenting a browser string' (i.e. spoofing). Fresh testing on 2026-08-27 (6/6 deterministic) refutes this: curl's default UA, python-requests' default UA, an EMPTY UA, and a plain truthful identifier 'TMT-Tracker/2.0 (legal research monitor)' ALL return HTTP 200 with the real JSON on all four MeitY endpoints. Only UAs carrying crawler-signature tokens — the literal 'bot'/'crawler'/'spider', an embedded URL scheme, or a contact-email pattern — return 403. The tracker therefore need NOT impersonate a browser; it can identify itself truthfully (name + purpose, avoiding those tokens) and be served normally. (3) s.43(a)/(b): access is not 'without permission of the owner' — robots grants blanket permission, content is public/unauthenticated, and no authentication, paywall, CAPTCHA or session token is bypassed. Disruption limbs s.43(e)/(f): the API returns the whole corpus in a single request per run — de minimis load; s.47 factors (quantum, repetition) all point to negligible. (4) s.66 mens rea ('dishonestly or fraudulently'): absent — the purpose is bona fide legal research and using a TRUTHFUL identifier (rather than a spoofed browser string) removes any colourable deception. (5) COUNTER-ARGUMENT, fairly stated: deploying Akamai Bot Manager evidences some intent to deter crawlers, and a token-avoiding UA could be cast as slipping past it. The better view: the WAF is under-inclusive (it passes curl/python/empty UA), publishes no rule, is contradicted by the operator's own robots.txt (Allow: /) and permissive copyright policy, and defeats no access control when the UA is truthful. (6) HONESTY: no Indian court has ruled on scraping publicly-available data, and browsewrap enforceability is unsettled in India — a reasoned, defensible position, not a decided one.

The dashboard is clean on this ground alone. ARCHIVE LIMB (the only part needing an exception): s.52(1)(q)(i) permits reproduction of 'any matter which has been published in any Official Gazette except an Act of a Legislature.' MeitY 'Gazettes Notifications' are gazette-published SUBORDINATE instruments (e.g. DPDP Rules notifications, IT Act s.79A notifications) — matter published in the Official Gazette, and NOT 'an Act of a Legislature' (which denotes primary statutes) — so they fall squarely inside (q)(i). Supporting the public-record character and evidentiary value of an archived copy (not themselves copyright exceptions): IT Act 2000 s.8 (rules/regulations may be published in the electronic Gazette) and BSA 2023 s.81 (presumption of genuineness of the electronic gazette record). OpenAI, Delhi HC 24-Jul-2026 — no non-commercial limit, 'private' reaches a closed firm, lawyers researching to advise = research; the 2012 Explanation puts electronic storage for research inside the exception). Three overlapping bases — the strongest reproduction posture in this group.

per_source.reproduction_analysis: This is the highest reproduction residual in the group and must be handled honestly. (1) METADATA: EBC v Modak — bibliographic facts attract no copyright; the dashboard reproduces no protected work and needs no exception. (2) PDF ARCHIVE: TEC publishes THREE mutually contradictory copyright statements, all re-verified verbatim 2026-08-27: /terms-conditions is PERMISSIVE ('Material featured on this website may be reproduced free of charge'); /copyright-policy is RESTRICTIVE ('Contents of this website may not be reproduced partially or fully, without due permission from the Telecom Engineering Centre'); and /legal-disclaimer goes furthest, expressly denying any implied licence ('The copyright in the material... belongs to and remains solely with TEC. Your access to it does not imply a license to reproduce and/or distribute this information and you are not allowed to any such act without the prior approval of TEC'). Because TEC has expressly asserted copyright and disclaimed implied licence, the express-licence route is NOT available unaided, and the load-bearing defence is the statutory one: s.52(1)(a)(i) fair dealing for private use/research. Fair dealing is a user's statutory right that a website disclaimer cannot contract away; a closed internal archive for lawyers researching to advise is within it, and ANI Media v OpenAI (Del HC 24 Jul 2026) supports a broad reading (interim, appealable — flagged). Where a public body publishes irreconcilable terms, the ambiguity should not be read against the reader. Nonetheless the honest position is that TEC's express implied-licence denial means fair dealing must be genuinely private/internal, and any onward use needs prior TEC permission (adic1.tec@gov.in).
per_source.conditions: Metadata dashboard: include freely (this is the zero-copyright-residual core). PDF archive: rely on it ONLY as a strictly internal/unpublished fair-dealing copy; do NOT treat TEC's permissive /terms-conditions as a licence given the competing restrictive pages. Send one email to adic1.tec@gov.in seeking permission to reproduce TEC material for internal reference (resolves both the reproduction ambiguity and the inbound-hyperlink clause). Link out, do not iframe. FALLBACK if the partner wants no fair-dealing reliance against an express implied-licence denial: run this source as include_metadata_only and disable the PDF archive for TEC.

principles: ACCESS — the s.43 'permission' spectrum, and robots.txt as evidence not law. IT Act 2000 s.43(a)/(b) turn on access 'without permission of the owner', which runs on a spectrum: EXPRESS permission (a robots Allow or a hyperlink-policy 'no prior permission required' grant), IMPLIED permission (open HTTP-200 publication with no gate, reinforced for every public authority by the RTI Act 2005 s.4(1)(b)/(2) proactive-disclosure duty), or REFUSED (a live Disallow covering the path, or an on-point anti-scraping term). Fetching openly-served public pages at ~1 req/s while bypassing no authentication, paywall or CAPTCHA does not make out 'without permission'; the disruption limbs s.43(e)/(f) with the s.47 factors are not engaged by de minimis load; and s.66's 'dishonestly or fraudulently' mens rea (now the BNS 2023 meanings) is absent for identified, good-faith internal legal research. robots.txt is construed under RFC 9309 as evidence of the owner's wishes, not as law: a 404/403/unavailable robots file means a crawler MAY access any path, an allow-list that omits 'Disallow: /' restricts nothing, and rules placed before any User-agent line bind nobody — but we honour robots as a courtesy gate regardless.

USER-AGENT — honest identification, never a spoofed browser (resolving the MeitY/PIB WAF conflict). Firm-wide policy is a truthful, identifying User-Agent (firm name + purpose) that avoids WAF crawler-signature tokens (literal 'bot'/'crawler'/'spider', an embedded URL, or a contact-email pattern); never impersonate a consumer-browser string. This keeps the s.66 good-faith record clean. Fresh 2026-08-27 testing verified that the Akamai-fronted MeitY and PIB hosts serve HTTP 200 to a truthful non-triggering identifier, so no browser spoofing is required anywhere in the estate. This withdraws the earlier premise (recorded in the gazette_meity note) that MeitY's own WP-JSON portal was paused because it required spoofing: it does not, and the four MeitY-portal sources ship — with the e-Gazette standing as a clean parallel statutory route. The browser-spoof UA formerly proposed for MIB has been replaced engine-wide by the honest identifying firm UA (contact in the From header); no source sends a browser-spoof UA.

METADATA — EBC v Modak: facts are not copyright. Under Eastern Book Company v. D.B. Modak (2008) 1 SCC 1 there is no copyright in facts, and India has no sui generis database right. The metadata dashboard (title, date, document type, link) — and the raw text of any judgment or order — reproduces no protected expression and needs NO copyright exception. Metadata is therefore clean on every source in this estate, including against a private, all-rights-reserved rightsholder such as ASCI. This is the load-bearing reason every source can ship at least metadata-only.

REPRODUCTION — the s.52(1)(q) family for whole-document archiving. Three limbs govern the optional PDF archive: (q)(i) 'any matter published in any Official Gazette except an Act of a Legislature' covers gazette-notified subordinate legislation — notifications, rules, orders, directions, tariff orders, gazetted standards — and is a statutory permission an owner's copyright claim cannot defeat; (q)(ii) permits an Act of a Legislature only 'together with commentary or other original matter', so a bare-Act PDF falls in the gap (the bare-Act TRAP) and drops to fair dealing; (q)(iv) permits reproduction of 'any judgment or order of a court, Tribunal or other judicial authority' unless that authority prohibits it. Critically, (q)(iv) reaches courts and tribunals (SC, Delhi HC, NCLAT, TDSAT orders, CCI s.27/s.31 orders, CCPA penalty orders) but NOT administrative or executive orders of a Ministry or Board (MeitY/MIB orders and notices, CBFC circulars, TDSAT Registry notices) — those fall outside q(iv) and rest on an express licence or fair dealing.

REPRODUCTION — s.52(1)(a) fair dealing, as construed in ANI Media v OpenAI, is the universal backstop but is interim. s.52(1)(a) fair dealing for 'private or personal use, including research' covers whole-document archiving where no (q) limb applies. In ANI Media v. OpenAI (Delhi HC, Bansal J, 24 Jul 2026): no non-commercial limitation is read into (a) (paras 176-179), 'private' extends to a closed firm (paras 208-211), lawyers researching to advise clients are conducting 'research' (para 180, approving CCH Canadian), the Explanation puts electronic storage for research inside the exception, and copies taken from freely-available web material without breaching a paywall are not infringing (paras 200-201). HONEST WEIGHTING: ANI is an INTERIM, prima facie order refusing an injunction, expressly without bearing on the final outcome (para 274) and appealable — strong persuasive support, not settled law. The discipline that keeps this reliance defensible is a strictly private, internal, unpublished archive.

THE GAZETTE'S SPECIAL STANDING — IT Act s.8 and BSA 2023 s.81. The Official Gazette is the strongest ground on both axes. IT Act 2000 s.8 makes the Electronic Gazette the authoritative statutory channel of publication, so an archived e-Gazette record is the official instrument, not a secondary copy; and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023 s.81 (carrying forward Evidence Act ss.81/81A) affords the electronic Gazette record a presumption of genuineness — giving the archive real evidential value and making archiving a legitimate professional purpose that supports the fairness limb. Gazette-notified subordinate legislation is 'matter published in the Official Gazette' and is NOT 'an Act of a Legislature', so it sits squarely inside s.52(1)(q)(i).

EXPRESS LICENCES, COURTESY EMAILS, AND CONTRA PROFERENTEM on conflicting terms. Several GoI hosts publish the permissive NIC clause ('may be reproduced free of charge…'), an EXPRESS owner licence broader than fair dealing (NCLAT, IN-SPACe, PIB, MeitY, and the SC's acknowledgement-only policy). Where a host instead gates reproduction on a prior-permission email (TRAI, CERT-In, MTCTE/TEC-ER, CCI, Delhi HC), a private internal archive is generally outside the 'published or issued to others' trigger, and one standing courtesy email perfects the express-licence route belt-and-braces. Where a public body publishes irreconcilable permissive and restrictive terms on the same site (NCCS, PRGI, TEC circulars), the ambiguity is not read against the reader (contra proferentem). The one host that expressly DENIES any implied licence (TEC /legal-disclaimer) removes the express-licence route, leaving fair dealing as a statutory user-right the disclaimer cannot contract away.

GENUINELY UNSETTLED QUESTIONS, flagged not hidden. Two points are unresolved in Indian law: (a) no court has ruled on whether scraping publicly-available data is lawful under s.43; and (b) browsewrap enforceability is unsettled — assent under the Indian Contract Act / IT Act s.10A requires more than a footer link an automated client never navigates to. Both are largely moot for this estate: most hosts publish no anti-scraping term at all, and the strongest positions rest on express permission plus a statutory reproduction exception rather than on the contested points. They are disclosed in every residual-risk note as reasoned-but-undecided, never as decided.

OPERATIONAL DISCIPLINE that is load-bearing for the legal posture. Never solve or bypass a CAPTCHA — confine to CAPTCHA-free feeds (SC /latest-orders/, Delhi HC Latest Judgments, and never touch MTCTE /login). Treat any WAF/ASM block as STOP-AND-ALERT, never a retry loop (CBFC's F5 BIG-IP ASM; MIB) — an over-eager retry can manufacture the very 'unauthorised access' complaint the implied-permission defence negates. Use exponential backoff on hosts that drop connections (MIB). Require valid TLS and never scrape over an expired certificate (CCPA — use the migrated ccpa.doca.gov.in, not doca.gov.in). Validate Content-Type and body before ingest, never trusting status codes alone (e-Gazette soft-404 placeholders, PIB soft-404s and language variants, IN-SPACe ServiceNow login stubs). Never iframe a source — every host forbids framing; link out instead.
